title: Figure.histogram: Let the parameter 'series' accept a sequence
body:
See https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/issues/4898 for context.

This PR implements a common function `_parse_series` to improve the `-T` option in `histogram`.

Now it's possible to use `series=np.arange(0, 10, 1)`, which is more familiar to Python users.

Example
```python
import numpy as np
import pygmt

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=100)
data = rng.normal(loc=100, scale=25, size=521)
fig = pygmt.Figure()
fig.histogram(
    data=data,
    frame=True,
    # series=5,
    # series=[0, 200, 5],
    series=np.arange(0, 200, 5),
    fill="red3",
    pen="1p",
)
fig.show()
```


Related to https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/issues/4251.

title: Accept numpy scalars for text's angle, Pattern's pattern and binstats' quantile_value
body:
**Description of proposed changes**

Several places validate numeric input with `isinstance(x, int)` / `isinstance(x, (int, float))`.
NumPy integers (`np.int64`, `np.int32`) and `np.float32` are not instances of `int`/`float`, so
they are handled inconsistently compared with the equivalent Python numbers:

- `Figure.text(angle=np.int64(30))` silently ignores the angle (no error, no `+a30` in `-F`).
  This is the worst case because there is no feedback.
- `Pattern(np.int64(15))` raises `GMTValueError: Invalid pattern number`.
- `binstats(statistic="quantile", quantile_value=np.int64(50))` (or `np.float32`) raises
  `GMTTypeError`.

This PR checks against `numbers.Real` / `numbers.Integral` instead, which NumPy scalars register
with. Booleans are explicitly rejected for `Pattern.pattern` and `binstats(quantile_value)`, since
`True` is an `int` in Python and previously produced `Pattern(True)` -> `'p'` (a pattern with no
number).

Tests added for all three.

title: Box, Position: Fix validation of shade_offset and refpoint
body:
**Description of proposed changes**

Two validation bugs in the new `pygmt.params` classes:

1. `Box(shade_offset=np.array([1, 2]))` raises `ValueError: The truth value of an array with more
   than one element is ambiguous`, because `shade_offset` is tested with plain truthiness
   (`if self.shade_offset and ...`, `self.shade_offset or []`). The same truthiness test makes
   `Box(shade_offset=[])` silently ignored rather than rejected as "not a sequence of two values".
   Now uses `is not None`.
2. `Position(["T", "L"], cstype="inside")` (or `"outside"`) raises `TypeError: unhashable type:
   'list'` from the `in _valid_anchors` set lookup, instead of the intended `GMTValueError`. Now
   checks `isinstance(refpoint, str)` first.

Tests added for both.

title: Fix sequence_join treating any string with a space as a datetime
body:
**Description of proposed changes**

`sequence_join` decided whether an item was datetime-like by checking for a space in `str(item)`, so any plain string containing a space was fed to `np.asarray(item, dtype="datetime64")` and raised `ValueError: Cannot create a NumPy datetime other than NaT with generic units`. Every `Alias(..., sep=...)` goes through this, so `magnetic_rose`/`directional_rose` crashed on free-text labels like `labels=["W", "E", "S", "Pole Nord"]` before GMT was called.

This replaces the space check with a type check (`datetime.date`/`datetime.datetime`/`pd.Timestamp`, or anything whose array dtype is `datetime64`, which covers `np.datetime64`, 0-d arrays and `xr.DataArray`). Plain strings are passed through unchanged. GMT itself accepts a space inside `+l` labels when the option is passed as a separate argv entry, so no escaping is needed.

Tested with the new `test_sequence_join_strings_with_spaces` (fails on `main`, passes here), the `sequence_join`/`alias` doctests, `test_helpers`, `test_alias_system`, and the magnetic/directional rose image tests, plus `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `mypy` on the changed files.

Fixes #4960

title: Figure.subplot: Expand the documentation of figsize and subsize
body:
**Description of proposed changes**

The docstrings of the `figsize` and `subsize` parameters of `Figure.subplot` were only one-liners. This PR expands them, following the current GMT `subplot` documentation (the text suggested in the issue is from GMT 6.2). They now describe:

- how the figure and subplot dimensions are derived from each other,
- how to set different widths/heights per column/row (`+f` fractions for `figsize`, comma-separated lists for `subsize`),
- how the subplot height is computed from `region` and `projection` for geographic maps (this only works with `subsize`, as in GMT),
- the modifiers `+a`, `+c`, `+g`, `+p` and `+w`.

I also changed the type lines from `list` to `tuple or str`, because strings are needed for the modifiers and lists, and the docstring example already uses a tuple. Happy to revert that if you prefer.

Only the docstring changes, no code.

How it was checked: I don't have GMT installed (Windows), so nothing was run against a real GMT. With Claude Code I checked that ruff, the pre-commit hooks, codespell and typos pass. I also checked that the docstring renders without docutils or Sphinx napoleon warnings. With the GMT session stubbed out, PyGMT builds the expected command lines (e.g. `-Ff10c/10c+f3,1/1,2` and `-Fs5c,8c/8c`). I compared the statements with the GMT docs and with GMT's `subplot.c`. comments.body:
How should we define an "AI assistant"? A wide spectrum of AI use cases exists:

1. Fully AI-generated content
2. AI-generated content subsequently reviewed and refined by humans
3. Human-authored content enhanced by AI
4. Human-authored content with AI help for docstring and comment refinement

We also usually can't know if a PR is done with AI assistant or not. Perhaps we should establish the AI policy first (https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/issues/4759)?
Based on https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/issues/4839#issuecomment-5446187833. But happy to revise this to set a threshold or something.
I think changelog entries should still contain contributions that have been AI-assisted. Hopefully not controversial?

Should we exclude commits that are AI-`Assisted-by` from the sorting? Just an idea, we can remove if not. I guess there are also PRs that are only partially AI-assisted, so this could be unfair to put.

This is a bit of a vague suggestion (sorry), but I do think setting the requirement for inclusion can be made a little less defined and state that the maintainers will add additional authors to AUTHORS.md in a PR. I think that having a hard limit of AI-assisted vs. non-AI-assisted can either incentivize lying about how AI was used, or can punish contributors for using AI in any way. While I don't think a contribution entirely from AI should merit inclusion as an author, I don't want to punish a contributor who meaningfully contributes but may use AI to either proofread or clean up their work. I realize that is hard to define, but I also think that is where maintainers' judgement can come into play when a contributor has been actively participating and a maintainer can submit a PR adding them to AUTHORS.md (and tag the contributor to make sure they want to be added).

Not that I expect pygmt to become insanely popular (we can dream!) but AUTHORS.md currently has 18 authors listed. I don't wish to set the bar high or come across as unwelcoming to new contributors, but I do think the list could be in the 30-40 range if the requirement is a single non-AI contributions, which seems longer than it should be.
Agreed; I think AI-assisted changes are still valid changes.

Similarly to my other [comment about maintainers' discretion](https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/pull/4871/changes#r3887986826), I think there should also be discretion in the sorting of the author list. I think lines of code is a good starting point and gives a rough idea of contributions, but I do think that it can incentivize longer contributions (e.g. tutorials, long documentation) that is useful, but isn't more useful than PRs with fewer lines of code.

My thought process is that if someone has contributed a few commits that were not AI-assisted, that means they have used enough brain muscle to understand the codebase themselves, and can reasonably be listed as an author. They could have still made AI-assisted commits, but the emphasis is that they should have made non AI-assisted ones to be eligible for authorship.

That said, I agree with the sentiment that (non-)AI-assisted is hard to tell nowadays and maybe it's time we switch to rely on a maintainer's judgement, maybe via a voting mechanism?

> it's time we switch to rely on a maintainer's judgement, maybe via a voting mechanism

I think this is a reasonable choice.

title: Figure.histogram: Improved syntax for filling bars by position/value
body: In `histogram`, bars can be filled by a constant color/pattern, or by the bin position or value (count, frequency). This is achieved by the `-C` option, with a syntax like `-C+b`. This PR implements a Pythonic syntax for such features by extending the existing parameter `fill` (alias of `-G`). In addition to color or pattern, now `fill` can accept two special values: `"position"` and `"value"`. ## GMT CLI and PyGMT comparison Here is a comparison: | GMT CLI | PyGMT | Notes | |---|---|---| | `-Gred` | `fill="red"` | Fill by a constant color | | `-Gp5` | `fill=Pattern(5)` | Fill by a pattern | | `-C` | `fill="position"` | Fill based on the current CPT and the mid-coordinate of each bar | | `-Ctest.cpt` | `fill="position", cmap="test.cpt"` | Same as above but use `test.cpt` | | `-C+b` | `fill="value"` | Fill based on the current CPT and the bin value (count or frequency, i.e., the bin height) | | `-Ctest.cpt+b` | `fill="value", cmap="test.cpt"` | Same as above but use `test.cpt` | ## Examples ``` import numpy as np import pygmt from pygmt.params import Frame, Pattern rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=100) mean = 100 # mean of distribution stddev = 25 # standard deviation of distribution data = rng.normal(loc=mean, scale=stddev, size=521) fig = pygmt.Figure() fig.histogram(data=data, frame=Frame(axes="WSen", title="Fill by color"), series=10, fill="green") fig.shift_origin(xshift="w+1") fig.histogram(data=data, frame=Frame(axes="WSen", title="Fill by pattern"), series=10, fill=Pattern(10, dpi=50)) fig.shift_origin(xshift="w+1") pygmt.makecpt(cmap="turbo", series=(0, 200, 25)) fig.histogram(data=data, frame=Frame(axes="WSen", title="Fill by position"), series=10, pen="1p", fill="position") fig.colorbar() fig.shift_origin(xshift="w+4") pygmt.makecpt(cmap="turbo", series=(0, 100, 25)) fig.histogram(data=data, frame=Frame(axes="WSen", title="Fill by value"), series=10, pen="1p", fill="value") fig.colorbar() fig.show() ``` ## Alternative implementation An alternative implementation is to keep `fill` unchanged, but alias `-C` to two separate parameters, `cmap` and `fill_by_value` (or any other names). The cons are: - User may be confused by the two similar parameters `fill` and `fill_by_value` - `-G` can't be used with `-C`, so we need to deal with conflicts between `fill` and `cmap`/`fill_by_value` carefully Address #4251

[ruff v0.17.0](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/releases/tag/0.17.0) introduces a breaking change to the rule `ICN001` (unconventional-import-alias), resulting failures in the Style Checks workflow (https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/actions/runs/38022301186/job/114125705838)
with errors like:
```python
unconventional-import-alias: `datetime` should be imported as `dt`
 --> doc/conf.py:7:8
  |
5 | """
6 |
7 | import datetime
  |        ^^^^^^^^
8 | import re
  |
help: Alias `datetime` to `dt`
   |
6  |
   - import datetime
7  + import datetime as dt
8  | import re
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
30 | author = "The PyGMT Developers"
   - copyright = f"2017-{datetime.date.today().year}, {author}"  # ruff: ignore[builtin-variable-shadowing]
31 + copyright = f"2017-{dt.date.today().year}, {author}"  # ruff: ignore[builtin-variable-shadowing]

The new codes still works with old ruff versions, so no ruff version bump here.

title: Figure.histogram: Add the parameter 'weights' for weighting data
body:
In `histogram`, `-Z+w` means using the second data column as weights. This PR provides the `weights` parameter which is more Pythonic. It can cover three use cases:

1. `data` is a file: `weights=True` means using the 2nd column as weights 
2. `data` is a 2-D array: `weights=True` means using the 2nd column as weights
3. `data` is a 1-D array: `weights` must be a 1-D array as weights

For comparison, [`matplotlib.pyplot.hist`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.hist.html) also provides the `weights` parameter.

Here is an example showing that PyGMT and matplotlib produce the same plot:
```python

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

plt.hist(data, weights=weights, bins=np.arange(0, 10, 1))
plt.show()


import pygmt
fig = pygmt.Figure()
fig.histogram(data=data, weights=weights, series=1, fill="lightblue", frame=True, region=[0, 10, 0, 0])
fig.show()
```

title: Figure.histogram: Improve parameters 'distribution' and 'distribution_pen' to draw distribution curves
body:
In `histogram`, the `-N` option draws the distribution curve. It's in the form of `-N[<mode>][+p<pen>]`, in which `<mode>` can be 0, 1, or 2 for different modes, and the option can be repeated when needed, and each curve can have different pen settings via `+p`.

Currently, `-N` option is aliased to `distribution`, so the syntax is like `distribution="0+p1p,red"`, `distribution=["0+p1p,red", "1+p1p,blue"]`. 

This PR proposes a new syntax with two parameters `distribution` and `distribution_pen`:

| GMT CLI | Old | New |
|---|---|---|
| `-N` | `distribution=True` | `distribution=True`* | 
| `-N1` | `distribution=1` | `distribution="median"` |
| `-N1+p1p,red` | `distribution="1+p1p,red"` | `distribution="median", distribution_pen="1p,red"`|
| `-N0+p1p,red -N1+p1p,red -N2+p1p,red` | `distribution=["0+p1p,red", "1+p1p,red", "2+p1p,red"]` | `distribution=["mean", "median", "lms"], distribution_pen="1p,red"` |
| `-N0+p1p,red -N1+p1p,blue -N2+p1p,yellow` | `distribution=["0+p1p,red", "1+p1p,blue", "2+p1p,yellow"]` | `distribution=["mean", "median", "lms"], distribution_pen=["1p,red", "1p,blue", "1p,yellow"]` |

*Supported for backward compatibility, but it's not recommended, because it's unclear which curve is drawn

**Example**
```python
import numpy as np
import pygmt
from pygmt.params import Axis, Frame

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=100)
mean = 100  # mean of distribution
stddev = 25  # standard deviation of distribution
data = rng.normal(loc=mean, scale=stddev, size=521)


fig = pygmt.Figure()
fig.histogram(
    data=data,
    frame=True,
    series=5,
    fill="red3",
    pen="1p",
    distribution=["mean", "median", "lms"],
    distribution_pen=["1p,blue", "1p,red", "1p,green"],
)
fig.show()
```

title: Figure.histogram: Add parameters to annote bars and deprecate parameter 'annotate'
body:
This PR provides a Pythonic implementation for the `-D` option. The GMT CLI syntax is:
```
-D[+b][+f<font>][+o<offset>][+r]
```
This PR maps it to multiple parameters

- `annot`
- `+b`: `annot_position` [default to `"top"`]
- `+f`: `annot_font`
- `+o`: `annot_offset`
- `+r`: `annot_orientation`

The prefix `annot` is preferred so that it's more consistent with `Figure.colorbar` and `Frame`. This PR also deprecates the `annotate` parameter to `annot`.

**Example**:
```python
import numpy as np
import pygmt
from pygmt.params import Axis, Frame

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=100)
mean = 100  # mean of distribution
stddev = 25  # standard deviation of distribution
data = rng.normal(loc=mean, scale=stddev, size=521)


fig = pygmt.Figure()
fig.histogram(
    data=data,
    frame=True,
    series=10,
    fill="red3",
    pen="1p",
    annot=True,
    annot_position="top",
    annot_font="8p,blue",
    annot_orientation="vertical",
    # horizontal=True, 
)
fig.show()
```

**Preview**: https://pygmt-dev--4895.org.readthedocs.build/en/4895/api/generated/pygmt.Figure.histogram.html

title: Figure.solar: Fix the bug that terminator datetime doesn't support fractional timezone offsets
body: **Description of proposed changes** As reported in https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/pull/4112 amd https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/gmt/issues/9220, GMT's `solar` module doesn't accept fractional timezone offsets like `08:30`. GMT always casts it to `8`. GMT already has a fix at https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/gmt/pull/9221. This PR adds a workaround on the PyGMT side, by always converting timezone-aware datetime to UTC datetime before passing to GMT. With this workaround, PyGMT works well for any GMT versions. This bug can be confirmed by the script below: ```python import pygmt import datetime fig = pygmt.Figure() fig.basemap(region="d", projection="W0/15c", frame=True) fig.solar(terminator_datetime="2020-01-01T01:02:03", pen="1p,black") fig.solar(terminator_datetime="2020-01-01T01:02:03+00:30", pen="1p,yellow,-") fig.solar(terminator_datetime="2020-01-01T01:02:03+01:00", pen="1p,red") fig.solar(terminator_datetime="2020-01-01T01:02:03-01:00", pen="1p,blue") fig.solar( terminator_datetime=datetime.datetime( 2020, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, tzinfo=datetime.timezone(datetime.timedelta(hours=2)) ), pen="1p,lightred", ) fig.solar( terminator_datetime=datetime.datetime( 2020, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, tzinfo=datetime.timezone(datetime.timedelta(hours=-2)) ), pen="1p,lightblue", ) fig.show() ``` Note the position of the yellow dashed line for a timezone offset `+00:30`. | Current main branch | This branch | |---|---| | | | Patches https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/pull/4112.

title: pygmt.show_versions: Simplify the parsing of __commit__
body:
Previously, `__commit__` is determined by parsing the `__version__` string with a long one-line code 
```
__version__.rsplit(sep="+g", maxsplit=1)[-1] if "+g" in __version__ else ""
```
. This PR simplifies it by using the `Version.local` attribute.

The new code `__commit__ = (Version(__version__).local or "")[1:]` works well for all possible cases, including release version, dev version, and dev version with dirty worktree, as shown below:
```python
In [1]: from packaging.version import Version

In [2]: __version__ = "0.1.2"

In [3]: (Version(__version__).local or "")[1:]
Out[3]: ''

In [4]: __version__ = "0.1.2.dev3+g0ab3cd78"

In [5]: (Version(__version__).local or "")[1:]
Out[5]: '0ab3cd78'

In [6]: __version__ = "0.1.2.dev3+g0ab3cd78.d20260924"

In [7]: (Version(__version__).local or "")[1:]
Out[7]: '0ab3cd78.d20260924'
```
For the last case (dev version with dirty worktree), `__commit__` contains the date information, so that it's distinguishable from the dev version with a clean tree.

~~The `actions/checkout` step takes 20 s for checking out the source code (see https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/actions/runs/35558719234/job/106207316870 for an example). It's slow because we have `fetch-depth: 0` (meaning fetch all Git history), which is required to have setuptools-scm work (xref: https://setuptools-scm.readthedocs.io/latest/integrations/#troubleshooting).~~

~~I asked Claude for help, and it suggested the `filter: blob:none` option, which perform a blobless clone (downloads all commit history and folder structures, but skips downloading actual file contents until you need them) (xref: https://github.blog/open-source/git/get-up-to-speed-with-partial-clone-and-shallow-clone/).~~

~~With this option flag, the `actions/checkout` step now takes 3 seconds only (https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/actions/runs/35599672884/job/106332531269?pr=4909).~~

It seems that setuptools-scm also provides such feature in https://github.com/pypa/setuptools-scm/pull/1303. I haven't tried it yet, but it seems we just need to add following settings to `pyproject.toml`:
```
[tool.setuptools_scm.scm.git]
pre_parse = "fetch_on_shallow"
```
However, such a feature is only available after [setuptools-scm v10.0.4](https://github.com/pypa/setuptools-scm/releases/tag/setuptools-scm-v10.0.4), which was released in March, 2026. So, setting this configuration means we need to bump the minimum required version for setuptools-scm.

```suggestion
    This method takes (longitude, latitude) values and reports the mean position and the
    pole to the great circle which best fits the input positions.

    Two methods are available to find the mean and pole positions, depending on the
    value of the ``norm`` parameter.

    - ``norm=1`` (L1 norm) approximates the minimization of the sum of absolute values
      of cosines of angular distances. This solution finds the mean position as the
      Fisher average of the data, and the pole position as the Fisher average of the
      cross-products between the mean and the data. Averaging cross-products gives
      weight to points in proportion to their distance from the mean, analogous to the
      "leverage" of distant points in linear regression in the plane.
    - ``norm=2`` (L2 norm) approximates the minimization of the sum of squares of
      cosines of cosines of angular distances. It creates a 3 by 3 matrix of sums of
      squares of components of the data vectors. The eigenvectors of this matrix give
      the mean and pole locations. This method may be more subject to roundoff errors
      when there are thousands of data. The pole is given by the eigenvector
      corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue; it is the least-well represented factor
      in the data and is not easily estimated by either method.

    When the data are closely grouped along a great circle both solutions are similar.
    If the data have large dispersion, the pole to the great circle will be less well
    determined than the mean. Compare both solutions as a qualitative check by calling
    :func:`pygmt.fitcircle`twice, once for each ``norm``.
